patient_information: A 4-year-old girl from Uganda, previously healthy.
chief_complaint: A 4-year-old girl presented unconscious after a 1-day history of headache, shaking chills, and a seizure.
history_of_present_illness: A 4-year-old girl, previously healthy, was well until the day before presentation. She had a bad headache in the early afternoon, and later in the evening developed shaking chills. Believing it was malaria, the family planned to take her to the health centre in the morning. At 5 a.m. on the day of presentation, the family found her in the midst of a seizure that lasted about ten minutes. It took 4 hours to reach the A&E department, and the girl had not awoken since the seizure. She has not had any recent head trauma.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from rural eastern Uganda, and it is the rainy season. Malaria is a common problem in their village.
vitals: Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse 150bpm, respiratory rate 36 breath cycles per minute and blood pressure 98/40mmHg. Capillary refill is normal.
physical_exam: She has no neck stiffness or jaundice. There is nasal flaring with respirations. Blantyre Coma Scale is 1/5. Pupils are 2mm and reactive, and extraocular movements are normal by oculocephalic manoeuvres. She has no papilloedema on direct ophthalmoscopy. With stimulation there is decerebrate posturing that resolves spontaneously. On cardiac examination she has a gallop rhythm. Her liver is palpable 2cm below the right costal margin and her spleen is 4cm below the left costal margin.
labs_and_diagnostics: A rapid test for glucose on admission was normal. Admission labs (Table 4.1) showed Haematocrit 17.6% (Ref: >30) and Platelet count 67 (x10^9/L) (Ref: 150–450). The Malaria RDT was positive. A lumbar puncture was performed; the CSF was clear and acellular, and the opening pressure was normal. Blood cultures were taken. Mydriatic drops were instilled, and ophthalmoscopy revealed white-centred haemorrhages in both eyes. An EEG showed diffuse slowing but no epileptiform activity.
differential_diagnosis: The most important underlying aetiologies of coma considered were cerebral malaria, acute bacterial meningitis, viral encephalitis, and intoxication (particularly organophosphates). Metabolic abnormalities (hypoglycaemia, or renal or hepatic failure) and non-convulsive status epilepticus were also considered. Although there was no neck stiffness, meningitis could not be ruled out in a deeply comatose patient. Rapid glucose testing ruled out hypoglycaemia, and the 4-hour gap since her last seizure made a post-ictal state unlikely. While the positive malaria RDT suggested cerebral malaria, this diagnosis is non-specific in high-transmission areas due to high rates of asymptomatic parasitaemia.
management_and_clinical_course: After a lumbar puncture and blood cultures, the child was administered artesunate 2.4mg/kg IV in A&E. She was admitted to the high-dependency section of the paediatric unit for frequent monitoring of vital signs and serum glucose. Artesunate was repeated at 12 and 24 hours, and then once daily. Twelve hours after admission, she had one short (1 minute) generalized seizure that spontaneously resolved. Forty hours after admission her Blantyre Coma Score was 4/5. The child was discharged home on hospital day five, with a follow-up appointment scheduled.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was retinopathy-positive cerebral malaria. This was based on the clinical presentation of an unexplained coma (Blantyre Coma Scale 1/5) in a 4-year-old child from a malaria-endemic area during the rainy season. Laboratory findings showed a positive malaria RDT, severe anaemia (Hct 17.6%), and thrombocytopenia (Platelets 67). The diagnosis was specifically confirmed by ophthalmoscopy, which revealed white-centred haemorrhages in both eyes, a key finding of malarial retinopathy. Bacterial meningitis was ruled out by the clear, acellular CSF, and non-convulsive status epilepticus was ruled out by EEG.
